**Claim.** Let $0<q<1$, $c\ge 0$, and suppose $a_{t+1}\le q\,a_t + c$ for all integers $t\ge 0$. Then for all integers $t\ge 0$,
$$a_t \le q^t a_0 + c\,\frac{1-q^t}{1-q}.$$

**Proof.** We argue by induction on $t$.

*Base case ($t=0$).* Since $q^0=1$,
$$q^0 a_0 + c\,\frac{1-q^0}{1-q} = a_0 + 0 = a_0,$$
so the claim holds with equality: $a_0 \le a_0$.

*Inductive step.* Assume for some $t\ge 0$ that
$$a_t \le q^t a_0 + c\,\frac{1-q^t}{1-q}. \tag{1}$$
By hypothesis,
$$a_{t+1} \le q\,a_t + c. \tag{2}$$
Because $q>0$, multiplying (1) by $q$ preserves the inequality, so
$$q\,a_t \le q^{t+1} a_0 + c\,\frac{q(1-q^t)}{1-q}. \tag{3}$$
Adding $c$ to both sides of (3) and combining with (2) gives
$$a_{t+1} \le q^{t+1} a_0 + c\,\frac{q(1-q^t)}{1-q} + c.$$
Now write $c = c\,\dfrac{1-q}{1-q}$, which is valid since $q\ne 1$, and combine the fractions:
$$c\,\frac{q(1-q^t)}{1-q} + c\,\frac{1-q}{1-q} = c\,\frac{q - q^{t+1} + 1 - q}{1-q} = c\,\frac{1-q^{t+1}}{1-q}.$$
Therefore
$$a_{t+1} \le q^{t+1} a_0 + c\,\frac{1-q^{t+1}}{1-q},$$
which is the claim for $t+1$.

By induction, the inequality holds for every integer $t\ge 0$. $\blacksquare$

*Remark.* The contraction factor $q<1$ is what makes the bound useful: as $t\to\infty$ the right-hand side tends to $c/(1-q)$. The proof itself uses only $q>0$ (to preserve the inequality when multiplying) and $q\ne1$ (to divide by $1-q$).
